newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Incentives help S.Korea's April car sales.
newsitem.headline: Incentives help S.Korea's April car sales.

text.p: South Korea's vehicle sales in April surged on a slew of incentives offered by car makers suffering from the slowing economy.
Sales on non-interest instalment payments were introduced by major producers in April, including Hyundai Motor Co Ltd, to boost domestic sales.
"The move, virtually a deep price cut, helped domestic car sales but was believed to have hurt profitability," said Sohn Jong-won, an analyst at Ssangyong Investment and Securities.
Company officials said the non-interest instalment sales were applied only to their employees, but analysts said the rule was not strictly imposed.
Hyundai Motor, South Korea's largest carmaker, said sales in April totalled 123,476 vehicles, up 12.9 percent from 109,354 in the year-earlier period.
Hyundai's domestic sales were 65,496 units against 64,524 a year earlier and exports were 57,980 against 44,830.
A Hyundai spokesman said exports improved in April due to the company's efforts to strengthen after-sales services and increase exports.
"Exports to Europe and Australia were especially good," he said. "Our sales focus shifted to exports because of the slowing domestic market.
Analysts said South Korean companies cut export prices to increase overseas shipments by around five percent.
"Korean car makers now are looking to exports as a way to tide over difficulties in the domestic market," said Nam Seung-soo, an analyst at Daishin Economic Research Institute.
"To compensate for sluggish domestic sales, car makers appear to be giving higher margins to their dealers overseas in addition to price cuts," Sohn said.
Kia Motors, South Korea's second-largest carmaker, reported sales of 72,353 vehicles in April, up from 68,373 a year earlier.
Its exports totalled 40,070 against 28,012 a year earlier and domestic sales 32,283 against 40,361, a statement said.
"Exports to the United States, Europe and Indonesia increased steadily in April," said a Kia spokesman, but he did not give details.
He said domestic sales were hampered by the slowing economy, which forced consumers to cut spending on durable goods like cars.
The recent introduction of new models by the nation's third-ranked Daewoo Motor Co. also affected Kia's domestic sales in the month, he said.
Daewoo began selling its Leganza mid-sized sedans in April.
Daewoo Motor, an unlisted unit of the Daewoo Group, said its vehicle sales in the month rose 13.7 percent to 69,988 units from 61,561 a year earlier.
Exports totalled 27,637 units in the month, down 17.8 percent from 33,615 a year ago, while domestic sales amounted to 42,351 units against 27,946.
A Daewoo spokesman said the rise in domestic sales was due to the successful debut of new models, including Leganza mid-sized sedans, which sold 14,151 units in April.
Sales of Nubira compact cars, which began selling in February, totalled 13,072 units in April and the smaller Lanos cars, rolled out last November, amounted to 5,160.
He said exports were affected by some shipping problems.
